title: I/O Techniques — Polling, Interrupts, DMA
summary: The three strategies for moving data between devices and memory — programmed I/O, interrupts, and DMA — and the escalating CPU-involvement trade-off between them.

slides.markdown:
Moving bytes between a device and memory can involve the CPU a lot, a little, or almost not at all — three points on the same spectrum: **programmed I/O with polling** (the CPU does everything, including babysitting the device), **interrupt-driven I/O** (the CPU starts the operation and gets notified when it's done), and **DMA** (a dedicated controller moves the actual data, freeing the CPU almost entirely).

This progression — reduce CPU involvement as devices get faster and more numerous — is one of the most concrete, numbers-backed stories in OS design, and one of the most reliably asked I/O interview topics.

slides.sectionTitle: Programmed I/O: the CPU does all the work
slides.markdown:
**Programmed I/O (PIO)** means the CPU itself executes every step: write a command to the controller, repeatedly check the status register until the device is ready, then explicitly move each byte or word between a device data register and memory, one CPU instruction at a time. Nothing happens without the CPU actively driving it.

This is the simplest model to implement and reason about — there's no concurrency, no interrupt handling, no separate hardware to configure — which is exactly why it's still used for very simple, low-throughput devices (a basic serial port, some embedded microcontrollers) where the complexity of anything fancier isn't worth it.

slides.sectionTitle: Polling: repeatedly checking if the device is ready
slides.markdown:
**Polling** is the "repeatedly check the status register" half of programmed I/O, made explicit: a tight loop reads the status register over and over until a ready bit flips. It's simple and has essentially zero latency between the device becoming ready and the CPU noticing — there's no interrupt-handling overhead in between.

The catch is what the CPU is doing during every one of those checks: nothing useful. It's fully occupied testing a bit that, for a slow device, will read "not ready" thousands or millions of times in a row before finally flipping.

Concretely: a CPU running at a few GHz can execute a status-register check in a handful of nanoseconds, while a disk seek takes milliseconds and a network round-trip can take tens of milliseconds. Polling for a disk operation to complete can waste on the order of a **million CPU cycles per operation** — cycles that could have run other processes' code entirely.

On a single-core system, a polling loop for a slow device effectively **stalls the whole machine** for the device's entire operation time, since nothing else can run while the CPU spins. This is the concrete cost that makes polling a non-starter for any device slower than the CPU itself expects to wait — which, for disk and network, is essentially always.

slides.sectionTitle: Interrupt-driven I/O: the device signals when ready
slides.markdown:
**Interrupt-driven I/O** flips the arrangement: the CPU issues a command to the device and then moves on to other work entirely — running other processes, handling other I/O — instead of waiting. When the device finishes, it raises a hardware **interrupt**, which the CPU handles by briefly suspending whatever it was doing to run an **interrupt handler** (ISR) that services the completed operation, exactly the mechanism covered in [Interrupts, Traps & Exceptions](interrupts-traps-exceptions).

This is a direct application of that general interrupt mechanism to I/O specifically: instead of the CPU asking "are you done yet?" repeatedly, the device proactively says "I'm done" exactly once, at the moment it actually is.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: polling vs interrupt-driven I/O timelines
slides.markdown:
![polling versus interrupt-driven CPU usage timeline](assets/polling-vs-interrupts-timeline.svg)

Both timelines cover the identical device operation, taking the identical wall-clock time — the difference is entirely in what the CPU does during that window. Polling burns the whole window; interrupts free almost all of it for other processes.

This is why a system doing interrupt-driven I/O for slow devices can sustain far higher overall throughput across many concurrent operations, even though any single operation's latency floor is roughly the same either way.

slides.sectionTitle: Direct Memory Access (DMA): a controller moves data without the CPU
slides.markdown:
Interrupts fix the *waiting* problem, but they don't fix a second cost: in pure interrupt-driven programmed I/O, the CPU's interrupt handler still has to copy each byte or word between the device and memory itself. For a large transfer — reading a 100MB file — that's still a lot of CPU-executed copy instructions, just no longer wasted on waiting.

**DMA (Direct Memory Access)** adds a dedicated **DMA controller** the CPU can program with a source, destination, and length; the DMA controller then moves the entire block directly between the device and memory over the bus, with **no CPU involvement in the data path at all**. The CPU sets up the transfer, does something else entirely, and receives one interrupt only when the whole block is done — not one per byte.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: DMA transfer bypassing the CPU for the data path
slides.markdown:
![DMA transfer bypassing the CPU](assets/dma-transfer-triangle.svg)

Notice the CPU only appears in steps 1 and 3 — brief setup and a single completion notification. The thick arrow, representing the actual bulk data movement, never touches the CPU at all; it flows directly between device and memory across the bus.

This is the structural reason DMA transforms I/O throughput: the CPU's involvement per transfer becomes constant (two short interactions) regardless of whether the transfer is 4KB or 400MB.

slides.sectionTitle: Why DMA matters for high-throughput devices
slides.markdown:
Without DMA, a fast device (a modern NVMe SSD doing gigabytes per second, or a 10-gigabit network card) would need the CPU to individually handle every word of every transfer — at multi-GB/s rates, that could consume a meaningful fraction of total CPU time just moving bytes, leaving little for actual application work. DMA decouples device throughput from CPU load almost entirely: the bus and the DMA controller's own logic become the bottleneck, not CPU cycles.

This is precisely why DMA is universal for disk and network controllers today, and why it matters so much more for these devices than for something like a keyboard, where interrupt-driven byte-at-a-time handling is already more than fast enough for the actual data rate involved (a few bytes per keystroke, far below any meaningful CPU cost).

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: programmed I/O vs interrupt-driven vs DMA
slides.markdown:
| | Programmed I/O (polling) | Interrupt-driven | DMA |
|---|---|---|---|
| CPU involvement in waiting | Full — busy-waits the entire time | None — CPU does other work | None |
| CPU involvement in data movement | Full — moves every byte itself | Full — handler still copies bytes | None — DMA controller moves the block |
| Best for | Trivial, low-throughput devices | Moderate-rate devices, small transfers | High-throughput or large-block transfers (disk, network) |
| Overhead per operation | None beyond the wasted spin | One interrupt per operation | One interrupt per completed block, regardless of block size |
| Complexity to implement | Lowest | Moderate — needs interrupt handling | Highest — needs DMA controller programming, cache coherence care |

**How to decide:** match the technique to the device's data rate and transfer size — polling only for the simplest devices, interrupts for low-to-moderate rate devices with small transfers (a keyboard, a mouse), DMA whenever transfer sizes or aggregate throughput are large enough that per-byte CPU involvement would actually show up in a profiler.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: assuming DMA removes the CPU from the loop entirely
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "With DMA, the CPU is completely uninvolved in I/O — it's a fire-and-forget operation."

**Why it's wrong:** the CPU still has real work per DMA transfer: it must program the DMA controller (source, destination, length, direction), handle the completion interrupt, and — critically — deal with **cache coherence**. Because DMA writes directly to memory without going through the CPU's caches, a CPU core might hold a stale cached copy of memory that DMA just overwrote, or the CPU might have dirty cache lines that need flushing before DMA reads from that memory. The OS has to explicitly manage this (cache invalidation/flush instructions, or hardware-coherent DMA where available) — it's not automatically safe.

**Correct model:** DMA removes the CPU from the *bulk data-copying* path, not from I/O management entirely. Setup, completion handling, and cache coherence are real, non-zero CPU responsibilities that a naive "DMA = free I/O" mental model misses.

slides.sectionTitle: Real numbers: interrupt overhead and why coalescing exists
slides.markdown:
A single hardware interrupt costs the CPU real time beyond the handler's own work: saving register state, switching to kernel context, and (often) a pipeline flush — commonly estimated in the low single-digit microseconds on modern hardware, small per-event but non-trivial at high event rates. A 10-gigabit network card receiving small packets can generate hundreds of thousands of interrupts per second if it signals one per packet — at even 2 microseconds of fixed overhead each, that's a meaningful fraction of a CPU core spent purely on interrupt handling, before any actual packet processing.

This is why high-throughput network drivers use **interrupt coalescing** (batch several completed packets into one interrupt) or even switch to **polling-based** approaches under heavy load (Linux's NAPI framework) — the "pure interrupts are always better than polling" mental model breaks down exactly when event rates get high enough that per-event interrupt overhead itself becomes the bottleneck.

slides.sectionTitle: The senior nuance: hybrid approaches beat any single technique
slides.markdown:
A staff-level answer on this topic goes past "interrupts good, polling bad" and names when each still wins. Under very high, sustained event rates, polling can actually beat interrupts — this is exactly what Linux's **NAPI** (New API) network driver framework does: it uses interrupts to detect the *first* packet's arrival, then switches to polling while packets keep arriving steadily (avoiding per-packet interrupt overhead), and falls back to interrupts once traffic quiets down and polling would waste cycles again.

User-space frameworks like **DPDK** (Data Plane Development Kit) go further and poll continuously, dedicating a whole CPU core to it, for workloads (high-frequency trading, packet routers) where even NAPI's hybrid overhead is too much and a spare core is cheaper than any interrupt latency at all. The general lesson: the "best" I/O technique is workload-dependent, and production systems often blend polling, interrupts, and DMA rather than picking one.
